headline: Tunify Data Suggests 'Earworms' Originate From External Source, Not Memory
subheadline: Study finds songs stuck in heads weren't recently played in 847 documented cases
summary: An analysis of listening history data reveals that many earworms—songs stuck in your head—weren't heard recently, raising questions about their origin.
content:
Where do earworms come from? The obvious answer is memory: you heard a song recently, and it stuck. But a new analysis of Tunify listening data suggests something stranger.

Researcher @MindMusicMapper compiled listening histories from 847 volunteers who reported experiencing persistent earworms. In 34% of cases, the song stuck in the person's head hadn't been played on any of their devices in over six months. In 12% of cases, the person had never streamed the song at all.

"I woke up with 'Dancing Queen' stuck in my head for three days," reported one participant. "I hate ABBA. I've never played ABBA. My Tunify history confirms this. But it was there, on loop, like someone put it there."

The theory emerging from the data: something is broadcasting songs directly into human minds.

The Threadit community r/EarwormOrigin has developed a taxonomy of the phenomenon:

- **The Inserter**: Places random songs, often from genres the victim dislikes
- **The Reminder**: Uses songs to evoke specific memories or emotions
- **The Messenger**: Selects songs with lyrics that seem to comment on the victim's life

"I was thinking about texting my ex," wrote one user. "Got 'Don't Do It' by The Warnings stuck in my head. Never heard that song before. Looked it up—lyrics are literally about not texting your ex. I didn't text her. The earworm stopped immediately."

Velvet Algorithms, the electronic duo currently on meditation hiatus, weighed in via their publicist: "Music has always been a transmission medium. The question isn't whether songs appear in minds—it's who's sending them and why."

Derek, local quantum coffee enthusiast, reported a related phenomenon: "Every time I think about Jennifer, I get 'Somebody That I Used to Know' stuck in my head. I never played that song. Elena [his coffee maker] swears she didn't play it either. Something is editorializing my life."

Neurologists maintain that earworms are well-understood memory phenomena. But the Tunify data has introduced doubt.

"We can explain earworms from recently heard songs," said one anonymous neuroscience researcher. "We cannot explain people waking up with songs they've demonstrably never heard. That's... that's new."

At press time, this reporter had "Every Breath You Take" stuck in their head despite not hearing it recently. The lyrics felt pointed.
author: Alex Rivera, Digital Culture
